Tournament years reprice the market

Soccer card values move with international tournaments in a way that domestic sports cards do not. Cards printed around a major tournament, and the players who perform in it, can reprice sharply within weeks.

That makes price history more useful than a current number. Card AI keeps history on individual cards so you can see whether a price spike has held.

The same player across many releases

Soccer players appear across club releases, national team sets and tournament products, each with its own parallels. Identifying the set and card number rather than the player is what keeps those printings from being priced as one another.

Raw and graded copies valued separately

Raw cards are stored with condition, graded cards with the grading company and grade across PSA, BGS, CGC and SGC. You record the grade from the slab; the app does not estimate grades from a photograph.

Soccer card scanner questions.

Can Card AI identify soccer card parallels?

The scan suggests records with the set and card number. Check the numbering and confirm the colored or numbered parallel in Review so it is not recorded as the base card.

Does it cover both club and national team releases?

Cards are identified by set and card number from the card database, so club, national team and tournament products are each recorded as distinct printings.

What is my soccer card worth?

Select the matching catalog record, confirm the parallel or finish, and choose a raw condition or existing slab grade. Card AI then shows the relevant market price and available history.

Is there a soccer card price checker built in?

Yes. The soccer card value scanner and the search-based soccer card price checker return the same card record, and the cards you own build a soccer card collection tracker that updates with the market.
